# 18.1 Finding Order in Diversity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Binomial nomenclature

Introduced in the **1730s** by the Swedish scientist **Carolus Linnaeus** — a **two-part scientific name in italics**, e.g. the polar bear, *Ursus maritimus*:

- **First word (capitalised)** — **genus**
- **Second word (lower case)** — **species**
- **Underlined if written by hand**

## Dichotomous key

A **dichotomous key** is **used to identify organisms**: a **series of paired statements or questions describing possible characteristics** of the organism, answered yes or no.

## Traditional and modern classification

**Traditional classification** is **based on morphology** — form and structure.

**Systematics** is the **science of naming and grouping organisms**. Its goals are to:

- **Organise living things into groups (taxa) that have biological meaning**
- **Assign each species a unique, universally accepted name**

**Modern systematics** **looks beyond simple similarities and differences** and **asks questions about evolutionary relationships**.

## The Linnaean classification system

Seven hierarchical taxa, from most to least specific:

**species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Binomial nomenclature** | A two-part scientific name of genus and species, written in italics |
| **Dichotomous key** | A series of paired yes/no statements describing characteristics, used to identify organisms |
| **Traditional classification** | Classification based on morphology — form and structure |
| **Systematics** | The science of naming and grouping organisms |
| **Taxa** | Groups into which living things are organised, having biological meaning |
| **Modern systematics** | Classification asking about evolutionary relationships rather than simple similarity |

# 18.2 Modern Evolutionary Classification

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Phylogeny

**Evolution** is **descent with modification**.

**Phylogeny** is the **study of evolutionary history**.

**Phylogenetic systematics** — evolutionary classification — groups species into **categories that reflect lines of evolutionary descent, rather than overall similarities and differences**.

## Cladistics

**Cladistics** is the **method of classifying species into groups called clades**, which **consist of an ancestor organism and all its descendants — nothing else**.

**Clades must be a monophyletic group**, including **all species descended from a common ancestor**.

**Cladistic analysis** shows that many taxonomic groups form clades — **Mammalia**, for instance.

A key example: the **clade Reptilia includes birds**, while **the Linnaean class does not** — because **crocodiles are more closely related to birds** than to other reptiles. This is the clearest case of morphology and descent disagreeing.

## Cladograms

A **cladogram** is a **tree diagram linking clades together**, showing **how evolutionary lines (lineages) branch off from common ancestors**.

- The **bottom (root)** represents the **common ancestor shared** by everything on the diagram
- **Branching points are nodes**, which **denote a speciation event** where a common ancestor split into two or more species
- **Branching patterns indicate degrees of relatedness** among organisms

## Derived characters

A **derived character** is a **trait that arose in the most recent common ancestor of a particular lineage and was passed along to its descendants**.

| Character | Clade |
|---|---|
| **Four limbs** | **Tetrapoda** — but **not derived for mammals** |
| **Hair** | **Mammalia** |
| **Specialised shearing teeth** | **Carnivora** |
| **Retractable claws** | **Felidae** (cats) |

The table shows why "derived" is relative to a lineage: four limbs is a derived character **for tetrapods** but tells you nothing about mammals specifically, since every tetrapod has it.

**Absence of a trait is not a derived character**, because **distantly related organisms can lose the same character**. Both **whales and snakes lost the tetrapod character of four limbs**, but **whales are in clade Mammalia and snakes in clade Reptilia**.

## Genetics in classification

**Genetics is the primary basis for grouping organisms into clades and determining paths of evolutionary descent**, and **DNA tools make this more accurate**.

**Because genes mutate**, shared genes carry information about how recently two lineages diverged.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Evolution** | Descent with modification |
| **Phylogeny** | The study of evolutionary history |
| **Phylogenetic systematics** | Classification grouping species by lines of evolutionary descent |
| **Cladistics** | The method of classifying species into clades |
| **Clade** | An ancestor organism and all its descendants, nothing else |
| **Monophyletic group** | A group including all species descended from a common ancestor |
| **Cladogram** | A tree diagram linking clades, showing how lineages branch from common ancestors |
| **Root** | The bottom of a cladogram, representing the shared common ancestor |
| **Node** | A branching point denoting a speciation event |
| **Derived character** | A trait arising in a lineage's most recent common ancestor and passed to its descendants |

# 18.3 Building the Tree of Life

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Changing ideas about kingdoms

| Date | Change |
|---|---|
| **1700s** | Linnaeus's original system divided all organisms into **plants (Plantae) and animals (Animalia)** |
| **Late 1800s** | **Protista** was added for microorganisms — protists and prokaryotes |
| **1950s** | **Monera** was added for prokaryotes, and **Fungi** was added |
| **1990s** | **Monera was split into Eubacteria and Archaebacteria** |

- **Prokaryotes** — **no membrane-bound organelles, no nucleus**
- **Eukaryotes** — **membrane-bound organelles, nucleus**

**Genomic analysis revealed that eukaryotes and the two prokaryotic groups are more different from each other than previously thought**, which required a new taxonomic category — the **domain**, a **larger, more inclusive category than a kingdom**.

**Kingdom "Protista" is a paraphyletic group — not a true clade.** **Only monophyletic groups are valid under evolutionary classification.**

The whole sequence shows classification responding to evidence: each revision came from better tools for seeing relationships, culminating in genomic analysis forcing a level above kingdom.

## The tree of life

Represents evolutionary relationships among the **three domains**.

### Domain Bacteria (Kingdom Eubacteria)

- **Unicellular and prokaryotic**, autotrophic or heterotrophic
- **Cell walls with peptidoglycan**
- Ecologically diverse; can be **aerobic** (requiring oxygen) or **anaerobic** (surviving only in the absence of oxygen)
- *E. coli*, cyanobacteria

### Domain Archaea (Kingdom Archaebacteria)

- **Unicellular and prokaryotic**, autotrophic or heterotrophic
- **Cell walls lack peptidoglycan**
- **Live in some extreme environments**; many are **anaerobic**
- Halophiles

The **peptidoglycan** distinction is the practical one: both domains are prokaryotic, and cell-wall chemistry separates them.

### Domain Eukarya

**Eukaryotic** — cells have a **nucleus containing DNA**.

| Kingdom | Characteristics | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Protista** | Mostly unicellular; autotrophic or heterotrophic; some have **cell walls with cellulose**. Some resemble fungi, plants, or animals. **Not a true clade** | Amoeba, brown algae |
| **Fungi** | Mostly multicellular, heterotrophic, **cell walls with chitin**. Most feed on **dead or decaying organic matter by secreting digestive enzymes** | Mushrooms, yeasts |
| **Plantae** | Multicellular, autotrophic, **cell walls with cellulose**, **non-motile** | Mosses, ferns, flowering plants |
| **Animalia** | Multicellular, heterotrophic, **no cell walls**, **mostly motile** | Sponges, worms, mammals |

Cell-wall composition distinguishes three of the four: **cellulose** in plants, **chitin** in fungi, **none** in animals.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Prokaryote** | An organism with no membrane-bound organelles and no nucleus |
| **Eukaryote** | An organism with membrane-bound organelles and a nucleus |
| **Domain** | A taxonomic category larger and more inclusive than a kingdom |
| **Paraphyletic group** | A group that is not a true clade, such as Kingdom Protista |
| **Peptidoglycan** | The cell-wall material present in Bacteria and absent in Archaea |
| **Aerobic** | Requiring oxygen to survive |
| **Anaerobic** | Able to survive only in the absence of oxygen |
| **Chitin** | The cell-wall material of fungi |

# 19.1 The Fossil Record

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A **fossil** is **the preserved remains or traces of ancient life**.

From the fossil record, **palaeontologists** learn about the **structure of ancient organisms, their environment, and the ways in which they lived**. Only a **tiny percentage become fossils, under special conditions**.

## Types of fossil

Fossils found in rock include **petrified fossils, moulds and casts, and trace fossils**.

| Type | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Petrified fossil** | **Minerals replace all or part of an organism** |
| **Trace fossil** | **Evidence of the activities** of ancient organisms — footprints, burrows |
| **Mould** | A **hollow area in sediment** in the shape of an organism |
| **Cast** | A **copy of the shape** of an organism |

Other fossils form when remains are **preserved in substances such as tar, amber, or ice**. **Amber fossils** form when organisms **become trapped in tree resin that hardens after the tree is buried**.

## How fossils form

Fossils are **usually found in sedimentary rock**.

1. **Sedimentary rock forms when small particles of sand, silt, clay, or lime muds settle to the bottom of a body of water**
2. **Sediment builds up and buries dead organisms**
3. **Over many years, water pressure gradually compresses** the layers into rock

## Dating Earth's history

**Relative dating** **places rock layers and their fossils into a temporal sequence**, determining whether a fossil is younger or older.

**Index fossils** are used to **establish and compare the relative ages of rock layers and the fossils they contain**. They:

- **Existed only in a few rock layers**
- **Occurred in large geographic areas**

**Trilobites** are the standard index fossil.

Both properties are required: a narrow time range makes the date precise, and a wide geographic range makes it usable for comparing distant sites.

**Radiometric dating** relies on **radioactive isotopes, which decay into non-radioactive isotopes at a steady rate**. It **compares the amount of radioactive to non-radioactive isotopes in a sample**.

**Half-life** is **the time required for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay**.

- **Carbon-14** has a half-life of **5,730 years**, and is **only useful for dating fossils no older than 60,000 years**
- The **most common** isotopes used are **potassium-40 and uranium**

The carbon-14 limit follows from its half-life: after enough halvings there is too little left to measure, which is why older samples need isotopes that decay far more slowly.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Fossil** | The preserved remains or traces of ancient life |
| **Petrified fossil** | A fossil in which minerals replace all or part of an organism |
| **Trace fossil** | Evidence of the activities of ancient organisms, such as footprints or burrows |
| **Mould** | A hollow area in sediment in the shape of an organism |
| **Cast** | A copy of the shape of an organism |
| **Amber fossil** | An organism trapped in tree resin that hardened after burial |
| **Sedimentary rock** | Rock formed when small particles settle and are compressed |
| **Relative dating** | Placing rock layers and fossils into a temporal sequence |

# 19.2 Patterns and Processes of Evolution

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Macroevolution and microevolution

- **Microevolution** — **change in allele frequencies that occurs over time within a population**
- **Macroevolution** — **grand transformations in anatomy, phylogeny, ecology, and behaviour**

## Macroevolution and cladistics

**Fossils are classified through shared derived characters**, and are **placed in clades** that either **contain only extinct organisms** or **include living organisms**.

The fate of a clade depends on two rates:

- **If the rate of speciation in a clade is equal to or greater than the rate of extinction, the clade will continue to exist**
- **If the rate of extinction exceeds the rate of speciation, the clade goes extinct**

## Patterns of extinction

**Background extinction** — extinction **because of the slow, steady process of natural selection**.

**Mass extinction** — **a relatively short period in which entire ecosystems vanish and whole food webs collapse**. **Natural selection cannot compensate quickly.** Causes include **volcanic eruptions, moving continents, and changing sea levels**; at the **end of the Cretaceous period, an asteroid crashed into Earth**.

The distinction is one of rate, and it matters because selection can keep pace with the first and not the second.

## Pace of speciation

**Gradualism** — **Darwin's** view, that **evolution occurred by a long sequence of continuous change**.
*Example:* the change in size and hoof of the modern horse.

**Punctuated equilibrium** — **long periods of relative stability in a species are punctuated by periods of rapid evolution**, with **no long sequence of intermediate forms**.
*Example:* the horseshoe crab. It is **much more common in organisms with short generation times**.

## Patterns of evolution

**Adaptive radiation, convergent evolution, and coevolution.**

**Coevolution** — **two species evolve in response to changes in each other over time**:

1. **Flowers and pollinators** — orchids with a long spur and moths with a long feeding tube
2. **Plants and herbivorous insects** — the **plant evolved bad-tasting or poisonous compounds**, and **insects evolved variants that could alter, inactivate, or eliminate the poison**

The second example shows the mechanism clearly: each side's adaptation creates the selection pressure driving the other's.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Microevolution** | Change in allele frequencies over time within a population |
| **Macroevolution** | Grand transformations in anatomy, phylogeny, ecology, and behaviour |
| **Background extinction** | Extinction through the slow, steady process of natural selection |
| **Mass extinction** | A relatively short period in which entire ecosystems vanish and food webs collapse |
| **Gradualism** | Darwin's view that evolution occurred by a long sequence of continuous change |
| **Punctuated equilibrium** | Long periods of stability punctuated by periods of rapid evolution |
| **Coevolution** | Two species evolving in response to changes in each other over time |

# 19.3 Earth's Early History

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Formation of Earth

Earth formed as **cosmic debris collided**.

**4.6 billion years ago:**

- **Violent volcanic eruptions**
- **Comets and asteroids bombarded** the planet

**4.2 billion years ago:**

- **Solid rocks** had formed
- **Water condensed** and fell as rain, forming **oceans with a great deal of dissolved iron**
- The **atmosphere had little or no oxygen**, consisting **principally of carbon dioxide, water vapour, and nitrogen**, with lesser amounts of **carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulfide, and hydrogen cyanide**

## First organic molecules

The **1953 Stanley Miller and Harold Urey experiment** suggested **how a mixture of organic compounds could have arisen from simpler compounds**.

## Formation of microspheres

**During the Archean Eon**, **large organic molecules formed tiny bubbles called proteinoid microspheres**.

Microspheres:

- **Have a selectively permeable membrane** for water to pass
- **Have simple ways of storing and releasing energy**

Those two properties are why microspheres matter: they are the minimum a structure needs before it can be called cell-like.

## Evolution of RNA and DNA

**The RNA hypothesis:**

- **RNA formed from simpler molecules and existed before DNA**
- **Simple RNA could lead to DNA-directed protein synthesis**

## Production of free oxygen

- **Prokaryotes were the first life form**, appearing **3.5 billion years ago**, in the **absence of oxygen**
- **Photosynthetic bacteria began producing oxygen 2.5 billion years ago**
- **Oxygen combined with iron in the ocean**
- **Oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, forming the ozone layer**

Note the order: oxygen was consumed by dissolved ocean iron before it could accumulate in the air, which is why free atmospheric oxygen lagged behind the organisms producing it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Miller–Urey experiment** | The 1953 experiment suggesting how organic compounds could arise from simpler compounds |
| **Proteinoid microsphere** | A tiny bubble formed from large organic molecules, with a selectively permeable membrane |
| **Archean Eon** | The period during which microspheres formed |
| **RNA hypothesis** | The proposal that RNA formed before DNA and could lead to DNA-directed protein synthesis |
| **Ozone layer** | The atmospheric layer formed as oxygen accumulated |

# 2.2 Properties of Water

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Polarity

There is a **greater probability of finding the shared electrons of a water molecule close to its oxygen atom** than near its hydrogen atoms.

The result is that the **oxygen end has a slight negative charge** and the **hydrogen end a slightly positive charge**.

A **polar molecule** is one whose charges are **unevenly distributed**. Every other property in this lesson follows from this one fact.

## Hydrogen bonding

Polar molecules such as water can **attract each other**.

A **hydrogen bond** is the **weak attraction between a hydrogen atom on one water molecule and the oxygen atom on another**.

## Cohesion and adhesion

**Cohesion** is attraction between molecules of the **same** substance. It produces **surface tension**.

**Adhesion** is attraction between molecules of **different** substances.

Two examples show the two forces competing:

- **Meniscus** — the adhesion between water and glass molecules is **stronger** than the cohesion between water molecules, so the surface curves up at the edges
- **Capillary action** — adhesion between water and glass causes water to **rise in a narrow tube against the force of gravity**

## Heat capacity

**Heat capacity** is the amount of heat energy required to increase a substance's temperature.

## Solutions

Water's polarity allows it to **dissolve both ionic compounds and other polar molecules**.

- The **solute** is the substance that is dissolved
- The **solvent** is the substance in which the solute dissolves

## The pH scale

The **pH scale** is a measurement system indicating the **concentration of H⁺ ions** in a solution, running **from 0 to 14**.

| Condition | Relationship |
|---|---|
| **Basic** | OH⁻ > H⁺ |
| **Neutral** | OH⁻ = H⁺ |
| **Acidic** | OH⁻ < H⁺ |

**The lower the pH, the greater the acidity and the less basic** the solution.

| **Polarity** | The greater probability of finding a water molecule's shared electrons near its oxygen atom than its hydrogen atoms |

| **Cohesion** | Attraction between molecules of the same substance |

| **Adhesion** | Attraction between molecules of different substances |

| **Capillary action** | The rise of water in a narrow tube against gravity, caused by adhesion |
| **Heat capacity** | The amount of heat energy required to raise a substance's temperature |
| **Solute** | The substance that is dissolved |

# 3.1 What Is Ecology?

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The biosphere

The **biosphere** consists of **all life on Earth and all parts of the Earth in which life exists**. It spans three physical realms:

- **Atmosphere** (gas)
- **Lithosphere** (solid)
- **Hydrosphere** (liquid)

It extends from about **11 km below sea level to about 8 km above** it — a thin shell, given the size of the planet.

## Ecology

**Ecology** is the **scientific study of interactions between organisms and their environment**.

## Levels of organisation

The six levels run from one organism up to the whole planet, each containing the one before it:

| Level | Definition |
|---|---|
| **1. Individual organism** | A **species** is a group of similar organisms that can breed and produce **fertile** offspring |
| **2. Population** | A group of individuals belonging to the **same species, area, and time** |
| **3. Community** | The assemblage of **different populations** living together in the same area |
| **4. Ecosystem** | Organisms in the same community **together with the physical environment** |
| **5. Biome** | A group of ecosystems that share **similar climates and typical organisms** |
| **6. Biosphere** | The entire planet's organisms **plus** the physical environment |

Note where the physical environment enters: a **community** is living things only, and an **ecosystem** is that community plus its non-living surroundings. That single step is the most commonly confused boundary in the list.

## Biotic and abiotic factors

- **Biotic** — living things
- **Abiotic** — non-living things

**The activities of organisms can influence abiotic factors**, so the two are not independent.

## Ecological methods

Ecologists work in three ways:

- **Observation** — using observations of natural phenomena to answer questions
- **Experimentation** — testing a hypothesis using designated processes
- **Modelling** — designing a model based on real situations to observe and answer questions

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biosphere** | All life on Earth and all parts of the Earth in which life exists |
| **Ecology** | The scientific study of interactions between organisms and their environment |
| **Species** | A group of similar organisms that can breed and produce fertile offspring |
| **Population** | A group of individuals of the same species, in the same area, at the same time |
| **Community** | The assemblage of different populations living together in the same area |
| **Ecosystem** | The organisms of a community together with their physical environment |
| **Biome** | A group of ecosystems sharing similar climates and typical organisms |
| **Biotic** | Living things |
| **Abiotic** | Non-living things |
| **Observation** | Using observations of natural phenomena to answer questions |
| **Experimentation** | Testing a hypothesis using designated processes |
| **Modelling** | Designing a model based on real situations to answer questions |

# 3.2 Energy, Producers, and Consumers

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Producers

**Autotrophs** are organisms that **use solar or chemical energy to assemble inorganic compounds into complex, energy-rich organic compounds**.

### Energy from the sun

**Photosynthesis** produces carbohydrates such as sugars and starches using **light energy**:

$$\mathrm{CO_2 + H_2O + light\ energy \rightarrow carbohydrates + O_2}$$

### Life without light

**Chemosynthetic bacteria** live in the deep sea, at volcanic vents, in hot springs, and similar places:

$$\mathrm{CO_2 + hydrogen\ sulfide + O_2 \rightarrow carbohydrates + sulfur\ compounds}$$

The two equations differ in one respect that matters: photosynthesis takes its energy from **light**, chemosynthesis from a **chemical** — which is why life is possible where no light reaches.

## Consumers

**Heterotrophs** acquire energy from other organisms. They are classified by what they eat:

| Type | Feeds on |
|---|---|
| **Carnivore** | Animals |
| **Herbivore** | Plants |
| **Omnivore** | Both plants and animals |
| **Scavenger** | The remains of other organisms |
| **Detritivore** | Detritus particles, which it **ingests** |
| **Decomposer** | Releases **digestive enzymes** |
| **Saprotroph** | Living or non-living organic matter — secretes digestive enzymes **into** it and absorbs the digested product |

Note the mechanism that separates the last three: a detritivore **eats** the particles, while decomposers and saprotrophs **digest externally** and absorb the result.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Autotroph** | An organism that uses solar or chemical energy to assemble inorganic compounds into complex, energy-rich organic compounds |
| **Photosynthesis** | Producing carbohydrates such as sugars and starches using light energy |
| **Chemosynthetic bacteria** | Bacteria producing carbohydrates without light, found in the deep sea, volcanic vents, and hot springs |
| **Heterotroph** | An organism that acquires energy from other organisms |
| **Carnivore** | An animal-eating consumer |
| **Herbivore** | A plant-eating consumer |
| **Omnivore** | A consumer that eats both plants and animals |
| **Scavenger** | A consumer that eats remains |
| **Detritivore** | An organism that ingests detritus particles |
| **Decomposer** | An organism that releases digestive enzymes |
| **Saprotroph** | An organism that secretes digestive enzymes into organic matter and absorbs the digested product |

# 3.3 Energy Flow in Ecosystems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Food chains and food webs

Energy flow is **one way**:

$$\text{Sun} \rightarrow \text{Producer} \rightarrow \text{Consumer}$$

A **food chain** is a **series of steps in which organisms transfer energy by feeding**. Food chains **vary in length**.

- **Phytoplankton** — primary producers that are a mixture of floating algae
- **Zooplankton** — small swimming animals that feed on marine algae

A **food web** is a **model representing interconnected food chains in which energy flows**.

The distinction is worth keeping precise: **food chains show how energy moves through an ecosystem, while a food web shows how food chains interact.**

**Decomposers** convert dead material to **detritus**, which **releases** and **recycles** nutrients.

## Balance of food webs

**Changes in the population size of one organism can disturb other organisms in the food web** — the reason a single removal can affect species that never interacted with it directly.

## Trophic levels

A **trophic level** is the **position of an organism in a food chain**:

$$\text{Producer} \rightarrow \text{primary consumer} \rightarrow \text{secondary consumer} \rightarrow \text{tertiary consumer}$$

## Ecological pyramids

An **ecological pyramid** is a **diagram showing the relative amounts of energy, biomass, or number of organisms at each trophic level in an ecosystem**.

**Pyramid of energy** — shows the relative amount of energy available at each trophic level, measured in **units of energy per unit area per unit time (kJ m⁻² y⁻¹)**.

**Transfer of energy is never 100% efficient. Around 90% of energy is lost** through:

- Not being eaten
- Not being digested or absorbed
- Being excreted
- Being lost as **heat from respiration**

That 90% loss is why food chains vary in length but cannot be very long — there is eventually too little energy left to support another level.

**Pyramid of biomass** — the relative amount of **living tissue** at each trophic level.

**Pyramid of numbers** — the relative **number of individual organisms** at each level.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Food chain** | A series of steps in which organisms transfer energy by feeding |
| **Food web** | A model representing interconnected food chains in which energy flows |
| **Phytoplankton** | Primary producers that are a mixture of floating algae |
| **Zooplankton** | Small swimming animals that feed on marine algae |
| **Detritus** | Dead material that decomposers convert, releasing and recycling nutrients |
| **Trophic level** | The position of an organism in a food chain |
| **Ecological pyramid** | A diagram showing relative energy, biomass, or numbers at each trophic level |
| **Pyramid of energy** | Shows the relative energy available at each trophic level (kJ m⁻² y⁻¹) |
| **Pyramid of biomass** | Shows the relative amount of living tissue at each trophic level |
| **Pyramid of numbers** | Shows the relative number of individual organisms at each level |

# 3.4 Cycles of Matter

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Recycling in the biosphere

**Energy enters as light** (trapped by photosynthesis) and is **usually lost as heat**, while **matter and nutrients are recycled**.

**Matter** is anything that takes up space and has mass. **Matter is never created or destroyed — it only changes.**

That asymmetry is the organising idea of the whole chapter: **energy flows through** an ecosystem and leaves, but **matter cycles within** it.

## Energy flow and nutrient cycles

- Energy enters from **sunlight**, and producers capture it
- Energy flows through the **trophic levels** of the food chain
- **Energy transfer is approximately 10% from one level to the next**
- Energy transfers to **detritivores or decomposers** in dead organic matter
- **Heat energy is lost through cell respiration**, and further energy is lost because material is not consumed
- **Nutrients** are absorbed by a producer from the ecosystem and move through the food chain by **digestion** of other organisms

## The water cycle

1. **Evaporation** — water → vapour. **Transpiration** is water loss from plant leaves
2. **Condensation** — cooling water vapour condenses into droplets around dust particles
3. **Precipitation** — rain, sleet, snow, hail
4. **Runoff** — the flow of water on the ground or underground
5. **Percolation** — gradual filtering through porous surfaces, also called **infiltration**

## Nutrient cycles

A **nutrient** is a **chemical substance that an organism must obtain from its environment to sustain life**.

### The nitrogen cycle

**All organisms require nitrogen for amino acids**, which are used to produce protein and nucleic acid.

**Forms of nitrogen on Earth:**

- **In air** — nitrogen gas (**78%**)
- **In soil** — ammonia/ammonium, **nitrate** (directly usable by plants), nitrites
- **In plants and animals** — organic nitrogen compounds such as protein

**The five steps:**

| Step | Process |
|---|---|
| **1. Nitrogen fixation** | Bacteria convert nitrogen gas into usable forms — **Rhizobium** in bean plants. **Lightning** converts a small amount as well |
| **2. Nitrification** | Soil bacteria convert ammonium into nitrites and then nitrates that producers can use |
| **3. Assimilation** | Plants absorb nitrate from the soil to make proteins and nucleic acids |
| **4. Ammonification** | Decomposers break down organic nitrogen compounds in dead organisms and release ammonium to the environment |
| **5. Denitrification** | Other soil bacteria convert nitrate back to **nitrogen gas** (and nitrous oxide) in the air |

Note that nitrogen gas makes up most of the atmosphere yet is useless to plants directly — step 1 is the bottleneck the whole cycle depends on.

### The phosphorus cycle

**Phosphorus forms part of vital molecules (DNA and RNA)** and is **not abundant in the environment**.

**Forms on Earth:** inorganic phosphate in land rock and soil minerals and in the ocean; organic phosphorus compounds in living things (DNA, RNA).

- **Short-term cycle** — phosphorus in phosphate solution is cycled from the soil to producers and then to consumers
- **Long-term cycle** — **weathering and erosion** of phosphorus-bearing rocks slowly adds phosphorus to the cycle

## Nutrient limitation

If ample sunlight and water are available, **the availability of nutrients may limit the primary productivity of an ecosystem**.

- **Primary productivity** — the rate at which primary producers create organic material
- **Limiting nutrient** — the nutrient whose supply limits productivity

In **marine ecosystems** nitrogen is typically limited; in **freshwater**, phosphorus. Some events cause a large input of limiting nutrients — **runoff**, for instance.

## Algal bloom

An **algal bloom** is a **dramatic increase in algae and other primary producers**.

The sequence: an increase in nutrients, with **not enough consumers** to match it, lets algae **cover the water surface** and **disrupt the function of the ecosystem**.

## Keywords

|---|---|
| **Matter** | Anything that takes up space and has mass; never created or destroyed |
| **Transpiration** | Water loss from plant leaves |
| **Condensation** | Cooling water vapour condensing into droplets around dust particles |
| **Runoff** | The flow of water on the ground or underground |
| **Percolation** | Gradual filtering of water through porous surfaces; also called infiltration |
| **Nutrient** | A chemical substance an organism must obtain from its environment to sustain life |
| **Nitrogen fixation** | Bacteria converting nitrogen gas into usable forms |
| **Nitrification** | Soil bacteria converting ammonium into nitrites and then nitrates |
| **Assimilation** | Plants absorbing nitrate to make proteins and nucleic acids |
| **Ammonification** | Decomposers releasing ammonium from dead organisms |
| **Denitrification** | Soil bacteria converting nitrate back to nitrogen gas |
| **Primary productivity** | The rate at which primary producers create organic material |
| **Limiting nutrient** | The nutrient whose supply limits productivity |
| **Algal bloom** | A dramatic increase in algae and other primary producers |

# 4.1 Climate

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Weather and climate

- **Weather** — the **day-to-day** conditions of the Earth's atmosphere
- **Climate** — **long-period patterns** of temperature and precipitation

Climate is **rarely uniform**. The factors affecting it are:

- Solar energy trapped in the biosphere
- **Latitude**
- Transport of heat by **winds and ocean currents**

Environmental conditions can vary over small distances — producing **microclimates**.

## Solar energy and the greenhouse effect

The **greenhouse effect** in three steps:

1. Solar energy arrives as sunlight and strikes the Earth's surface
2. Some of the solar energy is **absorbed and converted into heat**
3. Some heat radiates back into space, and **atmospheric gases trap some of it**

This **maintains Earth's average temperature**.

**Greenhouse gases:** CO₂, methane, water vapour.

Without the greenhouse effect, Earth's temperature would be about **30 °C different** — so the effect is not itself a problem; it is a precondition for life at habitable temperatures.

## Latitude and solar energy

- **Polar areas** receive **less** solar energy
- **Near the equator** solar energy is **intense**

This produces three **climate zones**: **tropical, temperate, and polar**.

## Heat transport in the biosphere

### Wind

In a **warmer region**, heated air **rises, expands, and spreads**, losing heat along the way; as the air cools, it **sinks**. In a **cooler region**, cooled air sinks and pushes surface air outward, where it warms.

**Earth's rotation** causes wind to blow generally **from west to east over the temperate zones** and **from east to west over the tropics and the poles**.

### Ocean currents

- **Warm surface currents** add moisture and heat to air
- **Cool surface currents** cool air
- **Deep water currents** are caused by cold water near the poles sinking and flowing along the ocean floor
- **Upwelling** — water rises in warmer regions

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Weather** | The day-to-day conditions of the Earth's atmosphere |
| **Climate** | Long-period patterns of temperature and precipitation |
| **Microclimate** | Local variation in environmental conditions over small distances |
| **Greenhouse effect** | Atmospheric gases trapping some radiated heat, maintaining Earth's average temperature |
| **Greenhouse gases** | CO₂, methane, and water vapour |
| **Climate zones** | Tropical, temperate, and polar |
| **Upwelling** | Water rising in warmer regions |

# 4.2 Niches and Community Interactions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Niche, resource, and tolerance

A **niche** is the **role or position an organism has in its environment** — where it lives, and how it interacts with that environment.

A **resource** is **any necessity of life**.

**Tolerance** is **the ability to survive and reproduce under a range of environmental circumstances**. Every species has its own range of tolerance.

Beyond or below the optimum range, organisms **experience stress**: they **expend more energy on homeostasis** and therefore have **less energy for growth and reproduction**. Tolerance **determines habitat**.

## Competition

**Competition** occurs when organisms **attempt to use the same limited ecological resource in the same place at the same time**.

- **Intraspecific competition** — within the **same** species
- **Interspecific competition** — between **different** species

Competition does three things:

1. Helps determine the **number and kinds of species** in a community
2. Determines the **niche** each species occupies
3. Causes species to **divide resources**

## The competitive exclusion principle

**No two species can occupy the same niche in the same habitat at the same time.** One species will be better at competing for the limited resource and will eventually **exclude** the other.

The consequence is not usually extinction but **division of resources** — which is why the principle and the observation below fit together.

**Dividing resources.** Among birds, one species may feed on high branches, another on middle branches, and a third on low ones.

## Predation, herbivory, and keystone species

**Predator–prey relationships** — an interaction in which one animal (the **predator**) captures and feeds on another (the **prey**).

**Herbivore–plant relationships** — an interaction in which an animal (the **herbivore**) feeds on producers. Herbivores can **affect both the size and distribution of plants**, and determine where certain plants can survive and grow.

**Keystone species** — a species that can **affect the entire ecosystem**.

The standard example: sea otters eat sea urchins, which feed on kelp. **Without sea otters, the urchins would eat all the kelp**, destroying food and habitat for other sea animals. The otter's importance is out of all proportion to its numbers, which is what "keystone" names.

## Symbiosis

**Symbiosis** is a **close relationship existing when two or more species live together**.

| Relationship | Effect | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Mutualism** | **+ / +** | Both benefit |
| **Commensalism** | **+ / 0** | One benefits, the other is unaffected |
| **Parasitism** | **+ / −** | One organism living in or on another benefits itself and **harms the host** |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Niche** | The role or position an organism has in its environment |
| **Resource** | Any necessity of life |
| **Tolerance** | The ability to survive and reproduce under a range of environmental circumstances |
| **Competition** | Organisms using the same limited resource in the same place at the same time |
| **Intraspecific competition** | Competition within the same species |
| **Interspecific competition** | Competition between different species |
| **Competitive exclusion principle** | No two species can occupy the same niche in the same habitat at the same time |
| **Predation** | One animal captures and feeds on another |
| **Herbivory** | An animal feeds on producers |
| **Keystone species** | A species that can affect the entire ecosystem |
| **Symbiosis** | A close relationship in which two or more species live together |
| **Mutualism** | A symbiosis where both species benefit (+/+) |
| **Commensalism** | A symbiosis where one benefits and the other is unaffected (+/0) |
| **Parasitism** | A symbiosis where one benefits and harms the host (+/−) |

# 4.3 Succession

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ecological succession

**Ecological succession** is a **series of predictable changes that occur in a community over time**. After disturbances, ecosystems change over time.

## Primary succession

**Primary succession** is the **establishment of a community in an area of exposed rock that does not have any topsoil**. It is **usually very slow at first**.

**Pioneer species** are the **first organisms to appear, growing on rock**. They:

- **Fix atmospheric nitrogen**
- **Break down rock**
- **Add organic material to create soil**

The absence of topsoil is what makes this slow: the pioneers have to **manufacture the soil** before anything else can grow, which is work that secondary succession never has to do.

The **end of primary succession is a climax community**.

**It often follows:**

- **Volcanic explosions** creating new land or sterilising existing areas
- **Retreating glaciers** leaving only bare rock behind

## Secondary succession

**Secondary succession** occurs when **existing communities are not completely destroyed by disturbances**. It is **faster than primary succession** — because the soil is already there.

**It often follows:**

- **Wildfire** — fires can stimulate seeds to grow
- **Hurricanes** or other natural disturbances
- **Human activities** such as logging or farming

## Climax communities

A **climax community** is an ecological community **in the final stage of succession**, in which the **species composition remains relatively stable until disturbance occurs**.

**Succession is not always the same path**, and climax communities are **not always uniform and stable**.

- **After natural disturbances** — secondary succession often produces the **original** climax community
- **After human-caused disturbances** — ecosystems **may or may not recover** from extensive human-caused disturbance

That contrast is the section's main claim: recovery is reliable after a fire, and not reliable after sustained human alteration.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ecological succession** | A series of predictable changes occurring in a community over time |
| **Primary succession** | The establishment of a community on exposed rock with no topsoil |
| **Pioneer species** | The first organisms to appear, growing on rock; they fix nitrogen, break down rock, and create soil |
| **Secondary succession** | Succession where existing communities were not completely destroyed; faster than primary |
| **Climax community** | An ecological community in the final stage of succession, relatively stable until disturbed |

# 4.5 Aquatic Ecosystems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Conditions underwater

Aquatic organisms are affected by **water depth, temperature, flow, and the amount of dissolved nutrients**.

### Water depth

- **Photic zone** — the **sunlit region near the surface in which photosynthesis can occur**, as deep as **200 metres** in tropical areas. It contains photosynthetic algae (**phytoplankton**) and **zooplankton**, which eat them
- **Aphotic zone** — **below the photic zone**, where photosynthesis **cannot** occur
- **Benthos** — aquatic organisms living **on or in rocks and sediment** on the bottom of lakes, streams, and oceans. Their habitat is the **benthic zone**

Where the water is shallow, **algae and rooted aquatic plants** grow. Below the photic zone, **chemosynthetic autotrophs are the only primary producers** — the same chemistry as 3.2, doing the job light cannot.

### Temperature, currents, and nutrients

**Currents can dramatically affect water temperature**, because they carry water that is significantly warmer or cooler.

**Nutrient availability** includes oxygen, nitrogen, potassium, and phosphorus; dissolved substances in water affect organisms.

## Freshwater ecosystems

Only **3% of Earth's surface water is freshwater**, but it provides terrestrial organisms with drinking water, food, and transportation.

Of total global water, **96.5% is ocean**, **2.5% freshwater**, and 0.9% other saline water. Of that 2.5%: **68.7% glaciers and ice caps**, **30.1% groundwater**, **1.2% surface or other freshwater**.

**Rivers and streams** — running water; organisms adapt to fast currents. **High oxygen level, little plant life.** Animals eat plants and other small animals.

**Lakes and ponds** — an inland body of **standing** water. Food webs combine plankton with attached algae and plants. Water flows in and out and circulates between surface and benthos, distributing **heat, oxygen, and nutrients**.

**Freshwater wetlands** — a **wetland** is an ecosystem in which water either **covers the soil or is present at or near the surface for at least part of the year**. Wetlands are **nutrient-rich and highly productive**, good for agriculture, and a breeding ground for many organisms. They help by:

1. **Purifying water** by filtering pollutants
2. **Preventing flooding** — absorbing large amounts of water and releasing it slowly

The **three main types** are **bogs, marshes, and swamps**, divided by vegetation.

## Estuaries

**Estuaries are saltwater wetlands**, formed **where a river meets the sea**, containing a **mixture of fresh and salt water**. They serve as **spawning and nursery grounds** for ecologically and commercially important fish species.

- **Salt marshes** — temperate estuaries, with salt-tolerant grass above the low-tide line and seagrass below water
- **Mangrove swamps** — tropical estuaries, with several species of salt-tolerant trees (**mangroves**)

## Marine ecosystems

Divided by **depth and distance from shore**.

**Intertidal zone** — organisms are **submerged at high tide and exposed to air at low tide**. Subject to changes in weather, and battered by waves and currents. The **rocky intertidal community** exists on exposed rocks of the shore, where **barnacles and seaweed permanently attach themselves**.

**Neritic zone (coastal ocean)** — from the low-tide mark to the outer edge of the **continental shelf**, the shallow border surrounding a continent. Water is supplied with nutrients in freshwater runoff, making it **highly productive**. It contains **kelp forests**, which live in cold, nutrient-rich water and grow up to 50 feet tall, and **coral reefs**, whose calcium-rich skeletons build up the reef.

**Open ocean** — from the edge of the continental shelf outward; **more than 90% of world ocean area**, at depths of **500 m to 10,000 m**. Divided by light penetration:

- **Photic zone** — low nutrient level, supporting the smallest species of phytoplankton. **Most photosynthesis occurs in the top 100 m**
- **Aphotic zone** — permanently dark. Its food web is based on material falling from the photic zone, or on chemosynthetic organisms. Organisms are exposed to **high pressure, frigid temperatures, and total darkness**, and some are **bioluminescent**

**Benthic environments** have high productivity, and **deep-sea vents support chemosynthetic primary producers**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Photic zone** | The sunlit region near the surface where photosynthesis can occur, to about 200 m |
| **Aphotic zone** | The region below the photic zone where photosynthesis cannot occur |
| **Benthos** | Aquatic organisms living on or in bottom rocks and sediment |
| **Benthic zone** | The habitat of the benthos |
| **Wetland** | An ecosystem where water covers the soil or is near the surface for part of the year |
| **Estuary** | A saltwater wetland formed where a river meets the sea, mixing fresh and salt water |
| **Salt marsh** | A temperate estuary with salt-tolerant grass and seagrass |
| **Mangrove swamp** | A tropical estuary with salt-tolerant mangrove trees |
| **Intertidal zone** | The zone submerged at high tide and exposed at low tide |
| **Neritic zone** | The coastal ocean, from the low-tide mark to the edge of the continental shelf |
| **Continental shelf** | The shallow border surrounding a continent |
| **Bioluminescent** | Producing light, as some aphotic-zone organisms do |

# 5.1 How Populations Grow

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A **population** is a **group of organisms of the same species that lives in a given area**.

## Estimating population size

**Sampling** is a technique used to estimate population size, in which organisms in a few small areas are counted.

**Random quadrat sampling:**

$$\text{Population size} = \frac{\text{mean number of organisms per quadrat} \times \text{total area}}{\text{area of each quadrat}}$$

**Capture–mark–release–recapture:**

$$\text{Population size} = \frac{n_1 \times n_2}{n_3}$$

where $n_1$ is the number initially caught and marked, $n_2$ the number caught the second time, and $n_3$ the number of marked individuals within $n_2$.

The formula rests on a proportion: the marked fraction of the second catch ($n_3/n_2$) should equal the marked fraction of the whole population ($n_1/n_0$).

## What researchers study

**Geographical range, density and distribution, growth rate, and age structure.**

**Geographical range** — the area inhabited by a population. Its size **can vary enormously depending on the species**.

**Population density** — the **number of individuals per unit area**. Numbers vary for different species in the same place.

**Distribution** — how individuals are **spread out across the range**. Three patterns: **random, uniform, or in clumps**.

**Growth rate** — determines whether a population increases, decreases, or stays the same. A **negative growth rate** means it is decreasing.

**Age structure** — the number of males and females of each age a population contains. Most **plants** cannot reproduce until a certain age; in **animals**, only females can reproduce.

## Factors in population growth

The factors are **birth rate (fertility or natality)**, **death rate (mortality)**, and **immigration/emigration rate**:

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| Immigration + natality **>** emigration + mortality | Population **grows** |
| Immigration + natality **=** emigration + mortality | Population **stable** |
| Immigration + natality **<** emigration + mortality | Population **declines** |

- **Immigration** — individuals move **into** the range from elsewhere
- **Emigration** — individuals move **out** of the population's range

## Exponential growth

**Exponential growth** occurs **under ideal conditions with unlimited resources**, producing a **J-shaped curve**.

- **Lag phase** — a slow growth period
- **Exponential growth** — the growth rate is **proportional to the size of the population**

## Logistic growth

**Logistic growth** occurs when a population's growth **slows and then stops**, following a period of exponential growth. Its growth curve is **S-shaped**.

| Phase | Characteristics |
|---|---|
| **Exponential growth phase** | Few predators; high natality, low mortality; plentiful resources, so no competition |
| **Transitional phase** | Predators increase and disease appears; natality decreasing, mortality increasing; competition for resources |
| **Plateau phase** | Immigration + natality = emigration + mortality, so the population is stable |

## Carrying capacity

**Carrying capacity** is the **maximum number of individuals of a particular species that a particular environment can support**.

It is limited by:

- Food and water availability
- Space for territories and nesting
- Availability of mates
- Disease
- Predation
- Environmental change

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Population** | A group of organisms of the same species living in a given area |
| **Sampling** | A technique for estimating population size by counting organisms in small areas |
| **Geographical range** | The area inhabited by a population |
| **Population density** | The number of individuals per unit area |
| **Distribution** | How individuals are spread across the range — random, uniform, or clumped |
| **Age structure** | The number of males and females of each age in a population |
| **Natality** | Birth rate, or fertility |
| **Mortality** | Death rate |
| **Immigration** | Individuals moving into the range from elsewhere |
| **Emigration** | Individuals moving out of the population's range |
| **Exponential growth** | Growth under ideal conditions with unlimited resources; a J-shaped curve |
| **Lag phase** | The slow growth period at the start of exponential growth |
| **Logistic growth** | Growth that slows and stops after a period of exponential growth; an S-shaped curve |
| **Carrying capacity** | The maximum number of individuals of a species that an environment can support |

# 5.2 Limits to Growth

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Limiting factors

A **limiting factor** is **a factor that controls the growth of a population**. Limiting factors **determine the carrying capacity** of an environment for a species.

## Density-dependent limiting factors

A **density-dependent limiting factor** **operates strongly only when population density — the number of organisms per unit area — reaches a certain level**. Such factors **do not affect small, scattered populations** as much.

### Competition

Individuals compete for **food, water, space, sunlight, mates, and other essentials**. The effects are **lower birth rates and increased death rates**, with **emigration increasing and immigration decreasing**.

This produces a self-correcting cycle: fewer individuals means low competition, so **immigration increases and emigration decreases**; that makes more individuals, so competition becomes high, and **immigration decreases while emigration increases**.

### Predation and herbivory

**Predator–prey relationships** — populations of predators and prey **cycle up and down, opposite to each other**.

**Herbivory effects** — populations of plants and herbivores likewise cycle up and down opposite to each other.

**Humans as predators** — human populations and the food they eat cycle up and down.

### Parasitism and disease

**The denser the host population, the more easily parasites spread** from one host to another.

### Stress from overcrowding

Overcrowding produces **fighting** and **high levels of stress**, which **weaken immunity**. Females may **neglect, kill, or eat their offspring**. The result is **lower birth rates, higher death rates, and increased rates of emigration**.

Every factor in this section shares one feature — it gets **stronger as the population gets denser**, which is what makes it density-dependent and what allows it to stabilise a population near its carrying capacity.

## Density-independent limiting factors

**Density-independent factors** reduce population size **regardless of density**. **Natural disasters — fires, floods, earthquakes —** are the standard examples.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Limiting factor** | A factor that controls the growth of a population and determines carrying capacity |
| **Density-dependent limiting factor** | A factor that operates strongly only once population density reaches a certain level |
| **Population density** | The number of organisms per unit area |
| **Density-independent factor** | A factor that reduces population size regardless of density, such as a natural disaster |

# 6.1 A Changing Landscape

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The effect of human activity

Three activities — **agriculture, development, and industry** — **affect the quality of Earth's natural resources**, including **soil, water, and the atmosphere**.

## Agriculture

**Monoculture** is **clearing large areas of land to plant a single highly productive crop year after year**.

Its impacts:

- Affects natural resources such as **water and soil**
- **Fertiliser production consumes fossil fuels**
- Increased use of **pesticides and insecticides**, which enter water and cause **biological magnification**

## Development

**Dense human communities produce large amounts of waste.** Waste that is **not disposed of properly affects air, water, and soil** resources.

Development also **consumes farmland** and **divides natural habitats into fragments**.

## Industrial growth

Industry **requires a great deal of energy** to power. **Burning fossil fuel affects the environment**, and **discarded wastes go directly into air, water, and soil**.

## Ecosystem goods and services

- **Services** — processes or actions that produce goods
- **Goods** — things that can be bought and sold, having value in dollars and cents

Where an **ecosystem cannot provide goods and services, society spends money to produce them**.

The worked example: streams, rivers, and lakes filter water naturally. When water quality falls, that service has to be replaced by **mechanical or chemical treatment** to provide drinking water — a free service becoming a paid cost.

|---|---|

# 16.1 Darwin's Voyage of Discovery

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The voyage

In **1831 Charles Darwin** set out on a **five-year voyage on the *Beagle***, mainly exploring the **Galápagos Islands**.

He developed a **scientific theory of biological evolution** explaining **how modern organisms evolved over long periods of time through descent from common ancestors**.

## Three patterns Darwin noticed

**Species vary globally.** Different, yet ecologically similar, animal species inhabit **separated but ecologically similar habitats** around the globe — the **emu** (Australia), **rheas** (South America), and **ostriches** (Africa).

**Species vary locally.** Different, yet related, animal species often occupy **different habitats within a local area** — the Isabella Island tortoise and the Hood Island tortoise, both in the Galápagos.

**Species vary over time.** Some **fossils of extinct animals were similar to living species**.

The three patterns work together: similar environments produce similar species that are *not* related, while nearby habitats hold related species that are *not* identical — and the same distinction appears across time as well as space.

## Ideas that shaped Darwin's thinking

**James Hutton and geological change.** Hutton proposed that **forces beneath Earth's surface can push rock layers upward**, tilting or twisting them. These processes are **very slow and take long periods of time**, from which he concluded that for them to have produced present-day Earth, the planet **must be much older than a few thousand years**.

**Charles Lyell's *Principles of Geology*.** Lyell argued that the **laws of nature are constant over time** and that **scientists must explain past events in terms of processes they can observe in the present** — **uniformitarianism**. The geological processes we see acting today must be the same ones that shaped Earth. He too argued that **Earth is very old**.

Both men mattered to Darwin for the same reason: evolution by small changes needs an enormous amount of time, and geology supplied it.

**Lamarck's evolutionary hypothesis — the inheritance of acquired characteristics.** **Jean-Baptiste Lamarck** suggested that **organisms could change during their lifetimes by selectively using or not using various parts of their bodies**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Evolution** | How modern organisms evolved over long periods through descent from common ancestors |
| **Uniformitarianism** | The principle that laws of nature are constant, so past events must be explained by processes observable in the present |
| **Inheritance of acquired characteristics** | Lamarck's hypothesis that organisms change in their lifetime by using or not using body parts |

# 16.4 Evidence of Evolution

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Fitness and survival of the fittest

**Fitness** is **how well an organism can survive and reproduce in its environment**.

**Survival of the fittest** is **the difference in rate of survival and reproduction**.

The crucial point about natural selection: **the environment influences fitness — not a farmer or an animal breeder.**

**Mimicry** is one strategy: a **harmless species mimics a harmful one**, as in grasshopper mimicry.

## Biogeography

**Biogeography** is the **study of where organisms live now and where they and their ancestors lived in the past**. It produces two contrasting patterns:

**Closely related but different — adaptive radiation.** One species evolves into several different forms that live in different ways, adapting to different environments. They **share a common ancestor**. Humans, cats, bats, and birds share a common ancestor: the first vertebrate.

**Distantly related but similar — convergent evolution.** Unrelated organisms live in similar environments and **come to resemble one another**, adapting to similar conditions. They **do not share a recent common ancestor**. Dolphins (mammals) and fish are the example.

The two are mirror images, and telling them apart is the whole skill: **similar ancestry producing difference**, versus **similar environment producing similarity**.

## Evidence 1: Fossils

**Earth is 4.5 billion years old.** **Intermediate fossil forms show the evolution of modern species from extinct ancestors.**

**Fossils** are **preserved or mineralised remains or imprints of an organism that lived long ago**. Because of geological processes, **marine fossils can be found on mountain tops**.

## Evidence 2: Comparing anatomy

| Structure | Definition | Evidence of common ancestor? |
|---|---|---|
| **Homologous structures** | Different species have structures adapted for **different functions** that nonetheless show **many similarities** — e.g. the five-digit forelimbs of tetrapods (amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) | **Yes** |
| **Vestigial structures** | Structures **inherited from ancestors** that have **lost much of their original function** due to different selection pressures on the descendant — e.g. the hind limbs of whales and dolphins | **Yes** |
| **Analogous structures** | Body parts that share a **common function but not a common structure** — e.g. the wing of a bee and the wing of a bird | **No** |

The distinction that matters: **shared structure** indicates ancestry, **shared function** does not.

## Evidence 3: Comparative embryology

**Similar patterns of embryo development** are evidence of a common ancestor. At some point in their development, **all vertebrate embryos exhibit common structures: a tail, a notochord, and pharyngeal pouches**.

## Evidence 4: Genetics and molecular biology

**All living organisms use the same universal genetic code.** Similarities in **DNA, RNA, and protein sequences provide the most powerful evidence** of common ancestry.

- **Homologous genes** — e.g. **Hox genes**, which help determine the head-to-tail axis in embryonic development. Homologous Hox genes are found in **almost all multicellular animals**
- **Homologous proteins** — e.g. **cytochrome c**, which functions in cellular respiration. Similar versions are found in **almost all living cells**

## Testing natural selection

Natural selection can be **observed in action** — in animals living in their natural environment, as with the **Galápagos finches**. The Grants' data also confirm the factors that drive natural selection:

- **Competition and overproduction**
- **Environmental change**
- **Sexual reproduction**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Fitness** | How well an organism can survive and reproduce in its environment |
| **Survival of the fittest** | The difference in rate of survival and reproduction |
| **Mimicry** | A harmless species resembling a harmful one |
| **Biogeography** | The study of where organisms live now and where they and their ancestors lived |
| **Adaptive radiation** | One species evolving into several forms living in different ways, sharing a common ancestor |
| **Convergent evolution** | Unrelated organisms in similar environments coming to resemble one another |
| **Fossil** | Preserved or mineralised remains or imprints of an organism that lived long ago |
| **Homologous structures** | Structures adapted for different functions that show many similarities; evidence of common ancestry |
| **Vestigial structures** | Structures inherited from ancestors that have lost much of their original function |
| **Analogous structures** | Body parts sharing a common function but not a common structure; not evidence of ancestry |
| **Homologous genes** | Corresponding genes across species, such as Hox genes |

# 17.1 Genes and Variation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Genotype and phenotype in evolution

An organism has **two sets of genes, one from each parent**.

**Alleles** are **specific forms of a gene**, which may vary between individuals.

- The particular **combination of alleles** an organism carries is its **genotype**
- The genotype **plus environmental factors** produces its **phenotype** — physical, physiological, and behavioural

**Natural selection only acts on phenotype.** That is the reason environment matters at all in evolution: selection can never see a genotype directly, only its expressed result.

## Populations and gene pools

A **population** is a **group of individuals of the same species that produce offspring**. Because they interbreed, they share a common group of genes — a **gene pool**.

A **gene pool** is **all the genes, including all the different alleles for each gene, present in a population**.

**Allele frequency** is the **number of times an allele occurs in a gene pool compared to the total number of alleles in that pool for the same gene**. It has **nothing to do with dominant or recessive**.

**Evolution involves a change in the frequency of alleles in a population over time**, and the changes it causes show up in the **population as a whole**.

## Sources of genetic variation

### Mutations

A **mutation** is **any change in the genetic material of a cell**.

- **Neutral mutations** do not change the organism's phenotype
- Mutations producing changes in phenotype **may or may not affect fitness**
- Mutations are what make an individual different from its parent

**Mutations matter in evolution only if they are passed from generation to generation.**

### Genetic recombination in sexual reproduction

**Crossing-over during meiosis:** paired chromosomes often **swap lengths of DNA at random**. This **increases the number of new genotypes created in each generation** and **explains why individual members of a species differ from one another**.

Note the division of labour between the two sources: **mutation creates new alleles**, while **recombination creates new combinations** of alleles that already exist.

### Lateral gene transfer

**Lateral gene transfer** is the **passing of genes from one organism to another**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Allele** | A specific form of a gene, which may vary between individuals |
| **Genotype** | The particular combination of alleles an organism carries |
| **Phenotype** | The genotype plus environmental factors — physical, physiological, and behavioural |
| **Population** | A group of individuals of the same species that produce offspring |
| **Gene pool** | All the genes, including all alleles for each gene, present in a population |
| **Allele frequency** | How often an allele occurs in a gene pool relative to all alleles for that gene |
| **Mutation** | Any change in the genetic material of a cell |
| **Neutral mutation** | A mutation that does not change the organism's phenotype |
| **Crossing-over** | Paired chromosomes swapping lengths of DNA at random during meiosis |
| **Lateral gene transfer** | The passing of genes from one organism to another |

# 17.2 Evolution as Genetic Change in Populations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The genetic definition

**Evolution is the change of allele frequencies in a population.**

**Fitness** means to **survive and reproduce** — that is, to **successfully pass genes to the next generation**.

## Natural selection on single-gene and polygenic traits

Both follow the same chain, differing only in how many phenotypes are exposed to selection:

- **Single-gene traits:** selection on a particular phenotype → change in allele frequencies → evolution
- **Polygenic traits:** selection on a **range** of phenotypes → change in allele frequencies → evolution

Each gene of a polygenic trait often has **two or more alleles**, so a single polygenic trait has **many possible genotypes and even more phenotypes**, and those phenotypes are **not clearly distinct**. Height and skin colour are examples.

## Three types of selection on polygenic traits

| Type | What is selected | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Directional selection** | **One extreme end** of the phenotype range | Industrial melanism in peppered moths |
| **Stabilising selection** | **Common or intermediate** forms, eliminating the extremes | Selection on birth weights of infants |
| **Disruptive selection** | **Both extreme ends**, eliminating the common forms — dividing one population into two distinct groups | Fewer medium-sized seeds means birds with unusually small or large beaks have higher fitness, producing two groups |

Disruptive selection is the one to watch, because it is the only one that **splits** a population — the starting point for speciation.

## Genetic drift

**Genetic drift** is a **random change in allele frequency**, usually in **small populations**, where individuals carrying a particular allele may leave more descendants **just by chance**.

Two types:

- **Genetic bottleneck effect** — due to a change in the environment (disaster, disease), **only a small portion of the population survives**, leading to a change in allele frequency
- **The founder effect** — due to the **migration of a small subgroup**; a few individuals become isolated from a larger population and establish a new one, whose allele frequency **differs from the original population's**

Both work the same way — a small sample of a population is not representative of it — and differ only in **why** the sample became small: most died, or a few left.

## Sexual reproduction and allele frequency

**Meiosis and fertilisation do not change the allele frequency of a population.** They produce **no new alleles**, only **many different allele combinations**.

## Genetic equilibrium and the Hardy–Weinberg principle

A population is in **genetic equilibrium** — and **does not evolve** — if **allele frequencies do not change**.

**The Hardy–Weinberg principle:** when a population is in genetic equilibrium, **allele frequencies remain constant from generation to generation**.

**Five conditions are required:**

1. **A large population** — genetic drift has less effect on large populations than small ones
2. **No mutation** — no new alleles introduced into the gene pool
3. **No sexual selection** — all members must have an equal opportunity to produce offspring
4. **No migration** — the population neither gains nor loses alleles by movement in or out
5. **No natural selection** — no phenotype has a selective advantage over another

Each condition is precisely the removal of one thing that causes evolution, which is why the principle works as a null model: **if allele frequencies do change, at least one of the five has been violated.**

## Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium

For a population in genetic equilibrium:

$$p + q = 1, \qquad (p+q)^2 = 1, \qquad p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $p$ | Frequency of the **dominant** allele **A** |
| $q$ | Frequency of the **recessive** allele **a** |
| $p^2$ | Frequency of genotype **AA** (homozygous dominant) |
| $2pq$ | Frequency of genotype **Aa** (heterozygous) |
| $q^2$ | Frequency of genotype **aa** (homozygous recessive) |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Evolution** | The change of allele frequencies in a population |
| **Fitness** | Surviving and reproducing — successfully passing genes to the next generation |
| **Directional selection** | Selection on one extreme end of the phenotype range |
| **Stabilising selection** | Selection on common or intermediate forms, eliminating extremes |
| **Disruptive selection** | Selection on both extremes, eliminating common forms and splitting a population |
| **Genetic drift** | Random change in allele frequency, usually in small populations |
| **Genetic bottleneck** | A change in allele frequency after only a small portion of a population survives |
| **Founder effect** | A change in allele frequency when a small subgroup establishes a new population |
| **Genetic equilibrium** | A state in which allele frequencies do not change, so the population does not evolve |
| **Hardy–Weinberg principle** | Allele frequencies remain constant across generations when a population is in genetic equilibrium |

# 17.3 The Process of Speciation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Species and speciation

A **species** is **a population or group of populations whose members interbreed and produce fertile offspring**.

**Speciation** is **the formation of new species**.

## Reproductive isolation

Speciation results from **reproductive isolation**, which arises in three ways:

| Type | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Behavioural isolation** | Two populations have **different courtship rituals** and other behaviours |
| **Geographic isolation** | Two populations are **separated by geographical barriers** — rivers, mountains, or bodies of water |
| **Temporal isolation** | Two or more species **reproduce at different times** |

All three produce the same result by different means: gene pools stop mixing.

## Speciation in Darwin's finches

The sequence has five stages: **founding of a new population → geographic isolation → change in the new population's gene pool → behavioural isolation → ecological competition.**

**1. Founders arrive.** Finches from South America (species M) arrive on the Galápagos Islands, survive, and reproduce. By the **founder effect**, the allele frequencies of the founding population could have differed from the original South American population.

**2. Geographic isolation.** Founder effect + geographic isolation + natural selection produce a new species (species A). Some birds from species A cross to another island — they fly over open water and move between islands only rarely, so they are **geographically isolated and no longer share a common gene pool**.

**3. Changes in gene pools.** Populations on each island adapt to the local environment. Plants on the first island produce **small seeds**; plants on the second produce **large seeds**, so **directional selection favours large beaks** for eating them easily. Natural selection causes the population to evolve large beaks — population B, characterised by that phenotype.

**4. Behavioural isolation.** If birds from the second island cross back to the first, they probably **will not breed**, because finches **choose mates by inspecting a potential partner's beak** and prefer to mate with birds of the same beak size. Differences in beak size plus mating behaviour produce **reproductive isolation**: the two gene pools remain isolated **even when individuals live in the same place**, and the populations have become **distinct species**.

Stage 4 is what makes the separation permanent. Geographic isolation alone is undone the moment the birds meet again; behavioural isolation survives contact.

**5. Competition and continued evolution.** As two species live together on the first island they **compete for seeds**. More specialised birds face **less competition** for certain foods, so **birds most different from each other have the highest fitness**. Over time, species evolve in ways that **increase the differences between them**, and species B may evolve into species C.

**Repeating** geographic isolation + genetic change + behavioural isolation produced the various finch species.

## Discussion

**Explain how disruptive selection can lead to the separation of a population into two distinct species.**

Disruptive selection concentrates the population at **both extremes** and eliminates the intermediate forms — which is the first step toward the two groups ceasing to interbreed.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Species** | A population or group of populations whose members interbreed and produce fertile offspring |
| **Speciation** | The formation of new species |
| **Reproductive isolation** | The separation of gene pools that produces new species |
| **Behavioural isolation** | Isolation caused by different courtship rituals and behaviours |
| **Geographic isolation** | Isolation caused by geographical barriers such as rivers, mountains, or water |
| **Temporal isolation** | Isolation caused by species reproducing at different times |
| **Founder effect** | Differing allele frequencies in a founding population compared with the original |
